summary: Specifies a base profile for X.509 v3 certificates and v2 CRLs for use with the United States National Security Agency's Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite, applying to US National Security Systems. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC sets rules for X.509 certificates and revocation lists used with the CNSA Suite. It limits which key types and signature algorithms can appear so different systems can interoperate.

questions: nsa commercial national security algorithm suite
subtitle: Certificate and revocation-list requirements for systems using the CNSA Suite.

tldr.problem: Systems using the CNSA Suite need compatible rules for X.509 certificates and certificate revocation lists.
tldr.mechanism: The profile restricts key types, curves, signature hashes, certificate versions, and required extensions.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC defines a base profile, not new cryptographic algorithms. Communities may define stricter profiles, while cross-community communication must meet the base profile.

today: RFC 8603 is an Informational RFC published in May 2019. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose of the CNSA Profile
sections.content:
RFC 8603 defines a base profile for X.509 version 3 certificates and version 2 Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) used with the United States National Security Agency's Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite.

The profile applies to US National Security Systems that use these certificates and is also appropriate for other US Government systems processing high-value information. It selects and constrains existing commercial algorithms rather than defining new ones.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC defines how certificates and revocation lists must be formed for systems using the CNSA Suite. It narrows choices already defined in other standards.

sections.title: Allowed Keys and Signatures
sections.content:
A CNSA Suite certificate must use an ECDSA signature-verification key or ECDH key-agreement key on curve P-384, or an RSA signature or key-transport key of 3072 or 4096 bits. Certificate and CRL signatures must use SHA-384.

For RSA signatures, the profile specifies RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5. It does not prohibit protocols from using RSA-PSS, but gives required parameters for those signatures. The profile also sets conditions on the RSA public exponent.
sections.plainLanguage: The profile allows P-384 elliptic-curve keys or RSA keys of the listed sizes. Every certificate and revocation-list signature uses SHA-384.

sections.title: Certificate Version and Public Keys
sections.content:
Certificates must use X.509 version 3, represented by the value 2 in the version field. For elliptic-curve keys, the certificate must use the id-ecPublicKey algorithm identifier and name the secp384r1 curve.

For RSA keys, the certificate must use the rsaEncryption algorithm identifier with NULL parameters and encode the public key as an RSAPublicKey. Implementations may use compressed or uncompressed elliptic-curve points, but relying parties must be ready to process the uncompressed form.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate must use version 3 and identify the key using the profile's required algorithm fields. Systems that read elliptic-curve certificates must accept the uncompressed point form.

sections.title: Required Certificate Extensions
sections.content:
Different certificates require different extensions. A self-signed CA certificate must include subjectKeyIdentifier, critical keyUsage with keyCertSign and cRLSign, and critical basicConstraints marking the subject as a CA.

Non-self-signed CA certificates require authorityKeyIdentifier, keyUsage, and basicConstraints. End-entity certificates require authorityKeyIdentifier and critical keyUsage, with digitalSignature for signature certificates or keyAgreement or keyEncipherment for key-establishment certificates. Policy extensions are required when a policy is asserted.
sections.plainLanguage: The profile requires different identifying and usage fields for CA and end-entity certificates. The required key-usage bits depend on whether a certificate signs or establishes keys.

sections.title: CRLs and Key Separation
sections.content:
CRL signatures must follow the same profile rules as certificate signatures. The profile also says a single key pair should not be used for both signatures and key establishment, following the cited NIST guidance.

Specific communities may add requirements or restrictions in their own profiles. When distinct communities need to communicate, they must conform to this base profile for interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: The same signature rules apply to revocation lists. Using separate key pairs for signing and key establishment is recommended, and the base profile remains the shared minimum between communities.
